title: Singapore Airlines Scripts Air India's Rescue Despite Only a 25% Stake
excerpt: The minority shareholder has absorbed nearly $800 million in losses and is being asked for a sizeable share of up to $1.5 billion in fresh equity as Air India's $2.3 billion loss forces Tata and SIA to fund the turnaround in milestone-linked installments.
body:
• Singapore Airlines, which owns just 25.1% of Air India, is driving the carrier's rescue — it has already booked about $780 million in operating losses on its bet and is now being asked to furnish a sizeable share of up to $1.5 billion in fresh equity, according to the Financial Times and Reuters.
  • Bloomberg reports Tata Sons and SIA are close to finalizing roughly $1.1 billion in support, to be released in installments tied to performance milestones — a sign the owners will keep funding the turnaround, but want results in return.
  • The scale of the hole: Air India Group posted a net loss of about $2.3 billion in fiscal 2026, more than double the prior year's $1.1 billion, with revenue down nearly 9%. Tata has sunk ₹45,347 crore into the carrier since taking ownership in January 2022.
  • Reader utility: SIA says Air India's customer-experience scores have improved sharply — its net promoter score is up more than 70 points since 2022 — but calls the transformation "a complex, multi-year programme" that will not be linear. Diaspora travelers should expect continued investment in cabins and service, alongside possible operational turbulence.

The minority owner doing the heavy lifting

Singapore Airlines holds only a 25.1% stake in Air India — yet it is SIA that is effectively scripting the Indian carrier's rescue. According to the Financial Times, SIA has booked operating losses of nearly $800 million over the two years of its investment, with more pain forecast. Reuters reports Air India has asked Tata Sons and SIA for up to $1.5 billion in fresh equity, with the minority partner expected to furnish a sizeable portion.

A separate Bloomberg report, detailed by Skift, says the two shareholders are close to providing ₹10,000 crore (about $1.1 billion) in new support — split by their 74.9/25.1 stakes, tied to performance milestones, and released in installments rather than a lump sum.

"Singapore Airlines remains committed to its multi-hub strategy and its participation in India's large and rapidly growing aviation market through its 25.1% shareholding in Air India."

— Singapore Airlines, in a statement to Reuters

How the turnaround derailed

When the Tata Group took over Air India in January 2022, the narrative was revival. Instead, the past year delivered a cascade of setbacks. The Air India Group reported a combined net loss of about ₹222 billion ($2.3 billion) in fiscal 2026, more than double the ₹108 billion loss a year earlier, while revenue fell nearly 9% to ₹718 billion ($7.5 billion).

The shocks are well documented: the June 12 crash of Flight AI-171 in Ahmedabad, a Boeing 787 bound for London that crashed into a college building shortly after takeoff, killing 241 people aboard and others on the ground; the prolonged closure of Pakistani airspace to Indian carriers after May's military clashes, which Air India says will cost it some ₹4,000 crore; the rupee's depreciation against the dollar; and high fuel prices compounded by the Middle East conflict costing the airline a key market.

Singapore watches its money

The rescue is politically sensitive in Singapore, where SIA is majority-owned by state investor Temasek. The funding request drew scrutiny in parliament, with opposition voices questioning the use of national-linked reserves to prop up Air India. SIA and the Singapore government have both pushed back: Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow told parliament the airline is "nowhere near" a scenario where its investment constrains its own fleet or network operations, and SIA said Air India funding comes from its internal resources under its capital allocation framework, with the full attention of the SIA board.

Meanwhile, Air India has a new hand on the controls. Tewolde Gebremariam, the former Ethiopian Airlines chief credited with building Africa's most profitable carrier, has taken over as CEO, with Tata signaling it wants group-wide operational muscle rather than just passenger metrics.

What it means for diaspora travelers

For the millions of Indian diaspora travelers who fly Air India between the U.S. and India, the rescue money matters at the cabin level. The funds are earmarked for systems upgrades, better engineering and in-house maintenance capabilities — exactly the operational weak spots passengers complain about. SIA points to real progress: Air India's net promoter score has risen more than 70 points since November 2022.

But the milestone-based funding structure is itself a message. Tata and SIA are willing to keep writing checks — SIA called it a long-term play on "India's large and rapidly growing aviation market" — yet the days of unconditional support are over. Travelers should expect continued improvement in service and reliability, but a turnaround this expensive and this complicated will not happen overnight.

What's next

Watch for the formal equity agreement in the coming weeks — and whether the milestone conditions are disclosed. The first installment will reveal how much urgency the owners attach to the turnaround. For Air India's passengers, the more telling signal will be fleet and maintenance investment: the in-house engineering capability the new funding is meant to build is the fix that actually reaches the seat.
